title: Getting Started: Setting Up the Time, Space, and Tools
hook: Before you can clear your head, you need a flat surface, a quiet hour, and a place for every loose promise.
counterintuition: Setting up trays, folders, and a work surface can look like avoidance when the pile is already urgent. In GTD, it is the first practical move, because a system cannot earn trust if capture and clarification are awkward from the start.
tryThisNow: Look at your calendar for the next hour. Identify one commitment you can write down in a trusted place. Do it now and notice how it feels to capture that thought.
keyTakeaway: When papers, texts, and receipts are tapping at you, first set up time, a clear surface, an inbox, a calendar, and folders, so each commitment is easy to capture and clarify.

breakdown.fastRead:
A Sunday night kitchen table tells the truth fast. Bills sit under crayons. A school form hides by the fruit bowl. Your phone has three notes named “remember.” None of this is work yet. It is loose stuff with nowhere trusted to go.

Before you try to get things done, give the stuff a place to land. Block real time. Clear one flat surface. Put an inbox, a pen, paper, files, and your calendar within reach.

Your head should notice commitments; the table, inbox, and calendar should carry the rest.
breakdown.deepRead:
By Thursday afternoon, a public defender can have four kinds of paper on one desk: hearing notices, client letters, court orders, and sticky notes with names written too fast. The danger is not only that something gets lost. A missed order can mean a client waits longer than necessary. The daily problem is that every item feels active because none of it has been parked where it can be checked.

Setup lowers the cost of telling the truth. If capture requires hunting for a pen, clearing a chair, finding the right folder, or deciding where a reminder belongs, you will postpone the decision. The loose item will stay half in the room and half in your head. A protected block of time, a real work surface, a physical inbox, a calendar, and plain folders do not do the work for you. They let you begin the work correctly.

The same problem follows a touring cellist after a weekend of concerts. A receipt is in a coat pocket. A presenter mentioned a possible spring date in a hallway. A student asked for repertoire suggestions by text. Without a small capture kit and a fixed review point after travel, those promises keep tapping on the glass. They interrupt practice, billing, and rest.

A good setup answers four blunt questions. Where does new stuff go? Where do reminders live? Where does support material wait? When will you look at the whole pile? If you cannot answer those, you do not have a system yet. Until those answers are visible, your memory is doing storage work it was never built to do.
breakdown.fullRead:
The trunk of a volunteer coach’s car can turn into a small office by accident. Cones roll under the stroller. Field permits curl in the side pocket. A half-used roll of athletic tape sits beside the snack list, and three parent messages are waiting on the phone while rain moves across the forecast. None of these items is dramatic. Together, they pull the coach’s attention away from the ten children kicking balls at midfield.

The useful question is not, what gear would make this look organized? It is, what job does each tool have? One tool captures, such as a small notebook or voice memo used the same way every time. One tool holds, such as a tray, folder, or bag section where loose paper cannot wander. One tool reminds, such as a calendar or next-action list. One tool stores, such as a reference folder for rosters, permits, and medical forms. If a tool has no job, it becomes cargo.

Setup needs time, space, and ordinary materials before the heavier thinking begins. Time protects you from pretending that setup can happen between two calls. Space lets you spread things out long enough to see what you actually have. Tools keep the decisions from fading after you make them. The method depends on trust, and trust is built by handling the same kind of input the same reliable way.

A charge nurse preparing for accreditation week faces the same shape of problem with higher stakes. Shift coverage, supply requests, compliance reminders, and patient-call follow-ups can all arrive through different doors. Some are clinical and urgent. Some are administrative and quiet until they are overdue. If all of them sit in memory, they start to sound equally loud. The wrong forgotten follow-up is not clutter. It can become a person waiting for care.

A modest control center changes the sound. An inbox takes loose notes. Calendar access holds the hard edges, the things that must happen on a certain day or at a certain time. Reference space keeps policies and phone trees from mixing with actions. Action lists separate what can be done on the phone, at the desk, during a supply check, or in a staff conversation. You are not admiring the station. You are making the next choice clean.

There is a trap here. Setup can become a hiding place. You can spend a whole afternoon labeling folders, rearranging trays, and testing pens while the actual pile waits untouched. That is just another form of delay. The test is whether the setup makes capture and clarification faster tomorrow. If it does not, make it plainer.

The opposite mistake is starting before the stage is set. A theater director two weeks before opening night may believe she can keep rehearsal notes, parent emails, costume problems, and facility requests moving through sheer attention. She cannot, at least not without paying for it during rehearsal. One reliable inbox for every loose commitment is not glamorous, but it lets the stage manager know where new issues land and when they will be handled.

Start smaller than your fantasy and more seriously than your habit. Protect a block of time. Clear a real surface. Gather the plain tools that catch, hold, remind, and store. Then begin emptying the scattered places into one visible flow. A setup has done its job when the question changes from where did it go to what does it mean?

examples.title: Maëlle Clears the Defender Table Before Court

planSpec.domain: a public defender preparing for a Friday morning case-backlog reset
planSpec.audience: an attorney whose desk is buried under hearing notices, client letters, and sticky-note promises
planSpec.stakes: whether court deadlines and client follow-ups remain scattered in memory or enter a place that can be reviewed
planSpec.requiredBeat: the attorney protects a setup block, clears a real work surface, and chooses simple trays and folders instead of treating a new tool as the solution

examples.scenario: Maëlle is alone in the public defender bullpen at 7:15 a.m. Thursday, one day before the case-backlog reset. Hearing notices, jail letters, and sticky notes cover her desk. She has blocked 90 minutes before arraignments, shoved two bankers boxes onto the floor, and cleared one metal table. A coworker texts a link to a case-management app. Maëlle is about to decide whether to download it now or set out three plain trays and manila folders first.
examples.whatToDo: Protect the 90-minute setup block, keep the table clear, and label simple trays and folders for inbox, active cases, waiting, and reference before opening any new software.
examples.whyItMatters: Court dates and client promises become reviewable only when they land in a stable physical flow. A new tool cannot help while paper still hides the next action.

examples.title: Mariko Sets the Rehearsal Inbox Before Notes

planSpec.domain: a high school theater director two weeks before opening night
planSpec.audience: a teacher juggling rehearsal notes, parent emails, costume problems, and facility requests
planSpec.stakes: whether dozens of small production commitments keep interrupting rehearsal because they have no single landing place
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director explains to a stage manager that the goal is not a prettier notebook but one reliable inbox where every loose commitment waits to be clarified

examples.scenario: Two weeks before opening night, Mariko stands in the black-box theater at 6:12 p.m., looking at a music stand stacked with parent emails, costume scraps, and a sticky note about the loading dock. Dante, her stage manager, holds up a fresh notebook. “Should I recopy everything by scene?” he asks. Mariko shakes her head. “Not a prettier notebook. One reliable inbox. Every loose promise goes there first, then we clarify it.” The cast is waiting, and she must decide whether to start rehearsal or protect ten minutes for setup.
examples.whatToDo: Protect the ten-minute setup block, clear the music stand, label one tray as the production inbox, and put every note, email printout, and facility request into it before rehearsal starts.
examples.whyItMatters: Production commitments arrive from many directions. A single landing place turns interruptions into a queue that can be clarified later, instead of letting each item compete with rehearsal.

examples.title: Lachlan's Red Tray After Bath-Time Chaos

planSpec.domain: a household with two preschoolers during a Sunday evening kitchen reset
planSpec.audience: a parent who finds bills, permission slips, library notices, and repair reminders in six rooms
planSpec.stakes: whether home administration keeps surfacing as background anxiety during meals, bedtime, and work calls
planSpec.requiredBeat: the parent moves scattered paper and notes into one visible household inbox and names the relief as trust in a container, not improved willpower

examples.scenario: Sunday at 7:18 p.m., Lachlan is wiping applesauce off the kitchen table while two preschoolers argue over bath toys. He is about to answer the preschool email from memory, then stops. Before the reset, papers wait on the microwave, in a backpack, under the couch, on his nightstand, in the diaper bag, and under a fridge magnet. He carries every bill, slip, notice, and repair note to a red tray beside the coffee maker. Afterward he says the quiet feeling is not better willpower, it is trusting the tray.
examples.whatToDo: Gather every loose home-admin item into one visible tray tonight. Do not sort yet. Clear enough counter space to process it, then decide each item’s next action when the children are down.
examples.whyItMatters: Scattered reminders force the brain to keep scanning rooms and replaying errands. One visible inbox gives every commitment the same entry point, so later clarification starts from a complete pile.

examples.title: Suyin Finds the Missing Capture Point

planSpec.domain: a touring cellist unpacking after a regional concert weekend
planSpec.audience: a freelance musician whose commitments are made in hallways, cars, green rooms, and text threads
planSpec.stakes: whether travel receipts, booking promises, repertoire notes, and payment questions disappear between cities
planSpec.requiredBeat: the cellist identifies the failure as missing portable capture tools and a review point, not as being disorganized or unserious

examples.scenario: Monday at 11:18 p.m., Suyin kneels beside her open cello case after three regional concerts. In the lining she finds two gas receipts, a wrinkled program with a conductor's booking promise, and a mute wrapped in a note about changing the Bach order. A venue manager has already texted twice about payment. Looking at the pile, Suyin sees the failure was not that she is careless or unserious. She had no portable capture tools, and no review point after the trip.
examples.whatToDo: Pack a pocket notebook, pen, and receipt envelope in the cello case. Block twenty minutes after each return to empty texts, notes, receipts, and promises into the same inbox.
examples.whyItMatters: Touring creates commitments away from the desk. If capture is not available at the point of promise, and review is not scheduled after travel, reminders scatter across bags, texts, and memory.

examples.title: Chinwe Builds a Clinic Corner Before Survey Week

planSpec.domain: a community clinic charge nurse setting up a small admin corner before accreditation week
planSpec.audience: a nurse responsible for shift coverage, supply requests, compliance reminders, and patient-call follow-ups
planSpec.stakes: whether operational commitments get mixed with clinical urgency until everything feels equally loud
planSpec.requiredBeat: the nurse creates a modest control center with an inbox, calendar access, reference space, and action lists while avoiding any sense that the setup itself is the achievement

examples.scenario: At 6:35 Monday morning, Chinwe, the charge nurse at Eastbank Community Clinic, wipes coffee rings from a two-foot counter beside the med fridge. Accreditation week starts tomorrow. She sets one wire tray for loose notes, opens the shared calendar on the old desktop, labels a binder shelf for policies and supply vendors, and tapes three plain action lists to the wall: Calls, Coverage, Orders. Then she steps back and leaves it unfinished enough to use.
examples.whatToDo: Set up the corner before the shift fills it: one inbox, calendar access, reference space, and visible action lists. Stop when each tool has a job, then start feeding it real commitments.
examples.whyItMatters: Clinic admin breaks down when reminders live in pockets, texts, and memory beside patient alarms. A small, trusted station separates operational work from clinical urgency so each can be reviewed at the right time.

examples.title: Natsuko Sorts the Trunk Before Kickoff

planSpec.domain: a neighborhood soccer coach using the trunk of a car as the season command post
planSpec.audience: a volunteer coach coordinating field permits, snack rotation, equipment, parent messages, and weather changes
planSpec.stakes: whether preventable logistics keep stealing attention from practices and games
planSpec.requiredBeat: the coach tests whether each tool has a job—capture, hold, remind, or store—so the setup stays practical rather than becoming gear collecting

examples.scenario: Natsuko is kneeling at the open trunk behind Field 3, Saturday 7:35 a.m., with cones, a pump, orange slices, the permit packet, parent texts, rain alerts, and a tempting sale page for a rolling gear bin on her phone. Before buying anything, she points to each item and asks what job it will do: capture, hold, remind, or store. She must decide whether the trunk needs more gear or clearer jobs.
examples.whatToDo: Assign each trunk tool one job: a pocket notebook for capture, a folder for permits and rosters, calendar alerts for reminders, and a bin for stored gear. Buy nothing without a missing job.
examples.whyItMatters: Field logistics fail when promises, papers, and equipment share the same pile. Job-labeled tools separate new inputs, fixed reminders, reference, and supplies so practice attention stays on players.

questions.prompt: A bakery owner finally has a quiet Monday afternoon to get control of supplier notes, staff requests, repair cards, and invoices. Which setup choice best supports the first real pass?
choices: Buy a complex scheduling tool and enter only the items that already feel urgent.
Protect the afternoon, clear a table, and set up a visible inbox, calendar access, and basic folders.
Leave the paper where it is and make a fresh to-do list from memory before customers arrive.
questions.explanation: The right first move is to reduce friction for capture and clarifying with time, space, and simple containers. A fancy tool or memory list skips the scattered commitments that are causing the noise.

questions.prompt: A university lab coordinator says, "I will trust my system once I find the perfect software." Meanwhile, grant receipts, equipment requests, and student notes sit in three bags. What is the best reply?
choices: Software choice should come first, because the system will fail unless the interface is pleasant.
The bags are fine for now, because visible clutter proves the work has not been forgotten.
Trust starts when every loose item has one landing place and a planned time to process it.
questions.explanation: The core issue is not software taste, it is reliable capture and review. The bags are not a trusted container, and a polished interface will not help if commitments never reach it.

questions.prompt: A wedding planner returns from a venue visit with napkin sketches, vendor promises, deposit questions, and text screenshots. She has 45 minutes before calls resume. What should she do first?
choices: Put every loose item into one inbox, note any missing capture points, and book a processing block.
Answer the easiest texts immediately so the pile feels smaller before deciding where things belong.
Create color-coded binders for each client, then sort only the items that match existing labels.
questions.explanation: She needs a clean intake path before action. Quick replies and attractive categories can feel productive, but they leave uncaptured commitments and unclear decisions loose in the system.

questions.prompt: A freelance photographer keeps losing model releases and location notes between shoots. He works from studios, trains, and cafes. Which change most directly fixes the setup weakness?
choices: Promise to be more careful at the end of each shoot and keep everything in his head until home.
Carry a simple capture kit and schedule a same-day point to empty it into his main inbox.
Buy a larger camera bag with more compartments so paperwork can be stored near the gear.
questions.explanation: Mobile work needs portable capture plus a transfer habit. Carefulness is not a system, and extra compartments can hide commitments unless they feed a reviewed inbox.

questions.prompt: A city inspector has a spotless desk, labeled drawers, and a new notebook, yet still wakes at night remembering permit callbacks. What is most likely missing?
choices: More storage categories, so each permit type has its own drawer and notebook section.
A stricter rule against taking new requests while old ones are still unresolved.
A reliable capture and review path that catches promises made in the field and turns them into next steps.
questions.explanation: Neat space is not enough if field commitments bypass the system. More categories or fewer requests may feel orderly, but the leak is uncollected promises with no review point.

questions.prompt: A novelist wants to "do productivity" before a book deadline. Her desk holds royalty letters, school forms, plot notes, and medical bills. What is the soundest opening move?
choices: Reserve a setup session, clear working space, and collect every loose item before deciding what each one means.
Start drafting at once and trust that nonwriting tasks will resurface if they matter enough.
Build a beautiful project dashboard for the novel and ignore household papers until the manuscript is done.
questions.explanation: A setup session lowers mental noise so writing can get clean attention. Waiting for tasks to resurface keeps loops open, while a novel-only dashboard leaves other commitments shouting.

questions.prompt: A small museum director has one Saturday to prepare for a fundraising season. Which plan is the best use of setup time?
choices: Spend the day redesigning the office so it feels inspiring, then begin collecting tasks next week.
Create a plain intake tray, reference area, calendar access, and action-list space, then process the current piles.
Invite staff to brainstorm goals for the year before touching donor letters, invoices, or event notes.
questions.explanation: The best plan equips the director to capture and clarify actual commitments now. Redesign and goal talk can help later, but they do not create a working intake path for today’s piles.

questions.prompt: An indie game studio holds a reset day. By noon, the team has installed a task board, but bug notes, publisher emails, and art requests remain in chat, notebooks, and memory. What problem should they name?
choices: The board is too new, so people need more time to enjoy using it before adding messy work.
The team lacks ambition, because important projects should not need reminders once agreed.
They installed a container without staging a complete collection sweep and a clear processing routine.
questions.explanation: A board only helps after commitments are gathered and clarified. Waiting for enthusiasm or blaming motivation misses the practical gap: scattered inputs have not been captured into one flow.

questions.prompt: A property manager gets maintenance requests by voicemail, hallway comments, email, and paper slips. Tenants complain about forgotten repairs. What setup choice will help most?
choices: Define one capture inbox for each input, keep tools nearby, and set a daily time to empty them into decisions.
Tell tenants to use only email, since reducing channels is always better than managing several inputs.
Hire another assistant before changing the request flow, because the problem is simply too much work.
questions.explanation: Multiple channels can work if each has a known landing place and a processing time. Email-only may ignore real conditions, and adding help will not fix a leaky intake flow.

reviewCards.front: You are eager to start your system, but your desk is buried and you have only ten spare minutes. What should you do first?
reviewCards.back: Do not start by processing random papers. Stage enough time, space, and ordinary tools to make capturing and clarifying commitments frictionless before you try to work the system. Protect a real setup block, clear a surface, and gather simple inboxes, paper, folders, and calendar access.

reviewCards.front: A clinic nurse sets up before accreditation week. Requests, callbacks, and supply notes are mixed with patient work. What setup move helps?
reviewCards.back: Create a modest control center before the week gets loud. Put an inbox where every admin commitment lands, keep the calendar and reference files close, and make action lists easy to reach. The setup is not the win. It only makes later capture and clarifying easier.

reviewCards.front: You find bills in the kitchen, a school form in the car, and a repair note by the bed. What should your home reset create?
reviewCards.back: Create one visible household inbox and put every loose paper or note there before deciding on each item. The relief comes from trusting one container, not from trying harder to remember. Once the pile has a home, you can clarify each item in order.

reviewCards.front: You are helping run a neighborhood meeting. Permits, speaker requests, and follow-up promises are scattered across texts and scraps. What do you test?
reviewCards.back: Test whether each tool has a job: capture, hold, remind, or store. If a notebook, tray, folder, or calendar does not reduce friction for one of those jobs, skip it. Build the plain setup that lets commitments land and be reviewed, not a collection of gear.

reviewCards.front: You keep buying new productivity tools, but your commitments still vanish between meetings. What is the check before adding another tool?
reviewCards.back: Ask what friction is still present. Do you lack protected setup time, a clear surface, a trusted inbox, calendar access, reference storage, or portable capture? Fix the missing condition first. A tool only helps if it makes capturing or clarifying commitments easier.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is preparing a small, reliable capture station before you ask your mind to calm down. You learn to protect time, clear a surface, and give each tool a simple job: collect, remind, hold, or store. When setup is plain and ready, loose commitments have a place to land before they turn into background noise.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you are about to start a backlog reset, then block 60 to 90 minutes, clear one work surface, and put every loose paper, note, and reminder into one physical or digital inbox before deciding what anything means.

If rehearsal notes, student questions, parent emails, or supply needs appear during class or practice, then capture each one in the same notebook, tray, or list and wait to sort them during a planned review time.
If you find bills, forms, receipts, or repair reminders in different rooms, then carry them to one visible household inbox and stop leaving them where you found them.

If you are coordinating a volunteer event from your car, bag, or kitchen table, then check that each tool has one job: a place to capture new promises, a place to hold papers, a calendar for dates, and a list for next actions.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, choose one spot where loose commitments usually pile up. Clear enough space for one tray, folder, box, or list, label it "Inbox," and put every nearby note, paper, and reminder into it without sorting yet.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, spend 20 minutes resetting your capture tools. Empty pockets, bags, counters, browser tabs, and stray notes into your inbox, then make sure your calendar, action lists, and reference storage are ready for the next week.

memorableLines.text: Before you can clear your head, you need a flat surface, a quiet hour, and a place for every loose promise.
memorableLines.why: This line succinctly captures the essence of preparation necessary for effective productivity, making it relatable and actionable.

memorableLines.text: Setup lowers the cost of telling the truth.
memorableLines.why: This surprising statement emphasizes the importance of organization in reducing mental clutter, resonating with anyone who has felt overwhelmed by disarray.

memorableLines.text: A setup has done its job when the question changes from where did it go to what does it mean?
memorableLines.why: This line offers a concrete test for whether setup is working, capturing the chapter's punchline about transformation from chaos to clarity.
